story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Hospice - Zip Data
story_ideas.headline: You can find out which hospices actually serve your address
story_ideas.angle: A zip-code lookup built from the CMS hospice service-area file, showing families how many Medicare-certified hospices cover their address instead of the one name they were handed.
story_ideas.hook: The service-area file refreshed 08/18/26 and makes each hospice's coverage territory public at the zip-code level.
story_ideas.consumer: Before you agree to the first hospice a discharge planner names, pull every hospice whose service area includes your zip code and put the same questions to each one.
story_ideas.b2b: Overlapping service areas at zip level are a competitive density map, and operators can see where referral sources have a genuine choice and where they do not.
story_ideas.why: A family that never learns a second hospice covers their address accepts the first one by default.
story_ideas.note: Localizable to states and counties; a coverage-count-per-zip map is the obvious chart.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Hospice care - State CAHPS Hospice Survey Data
story_ideas.headline: Your state's hospices scored this on the family survey
story_ideas.angle: A state-by-state ranking of mean CAHPS Hospice Survey scores, written for readers who want to know whether hospice care where they live typically rates well.
story_ideas.hook: State means refreshed 08/07/26 on the same date as the national and provider-level files, so the three levels can be compared without vintage mismatch.
story_ideas.consumer: Look up your state's average first, then ask the hospice you are considering how its own survey scores compare with that number.
story_ideas.b2b: Providers in low-scoring states carry a market-level reputation problem their own scores may not deserve, and state associations can now quantify it.
story_ideas.why: Knowing the state mean turns a provider's score from an abstract number into a pass or fail.
story_ideas.note: Fifty-state table; strong chart potential and a natural localization for regional outlets.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Hospice - General Information
story_ideas.headline: Who owns the hospice at your bedside is a published fact
story_ideas.angle: A walk through the hospice general information file, which carries address, phone number and ownership data, for families who have never thought to ask who runs the agency coming into their home.
story_ideas.hook: The file refreshed 08/19/26 and puts ownership alongside contact details for hospice providers, the same way nursing home ownership has long been public.
story_ideas.consumer: Check the ownership line for the hospice you are offered, and ask what else the owner operates in your area.
story_ideas.b2b: Ownership visibility at provider level changes how acquisitions and multi-site operators are perceived by referral partners.
story_ideas.why: Ownership tells a family whether they are dealing with a single local agency or one site in a chain, which shapes who answers when something goes wrong.
story_ideas.note: Joins to the zip and CAHPS files; localizable to states and counties.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Nursing Home Data Collection Intervals
story_ideas.headline: How old is the data behind that star rating?
story_ideas.angle: A plain reading of the intervals file, which lists the collection periods behind nursing home quality measures, complaint citations, focused infection control inspections and the staffing measures, for families treating a rating as current.
story_ideas.hook: The file refreshed 08/01/26 and states outright that some short-stay measures use different collection periods than others.
story_ideas.consumer: Before you judge a facility by its rating, check what period the measures behind it were collected over, then ask the administrator what has changed since.
story_ideas.b2b: Operators who improved recently are still being judged on an older collection window, and the intervals file is the document that proves it.
story_ideas.why: A family comparing two homes on scores drawn from different periods is comparing two different points in time.
story_ideas.note: Never worked as a story on its own; the lag chart is simple and reusable.

story_ideas.title: CMS refreshed dataset: Patient-Reported Outcomes - Hospital
story_ideas.headline: What patients say about walking, thinking and pain after a hospital stay
story_ideas.angle: A look at the patient-reported outcomes file, which collects what patients themselves say about pain management, functional ability and quality of life, for readers weighing a hospital before a planned procedure.
story_ideas.hook: The file refreshed 08/05/26 and records outcomes as patients describe them rather than as a facility reports them.
story_ideas.consumer: Ask about function, not just survival: whether patients like you came out able to walk, think and manage pain is a question this file was built to answer.
story_ideas.b2b: Self-reported function is a different quality currency than clinical measures, and discharge partners will start being compared on it.
story_ideas.why: An older patient choosing where to have a procedure cares most about the outcome this file measures and least about the ones usually published.

story_ideas.title: New EBRI Report Finds Some Medicare Households May Need Nearly $500,000 for Health Care in Retirement
story_ideas.headline: Some Medicare households may need nearly $500,000 for health care
story_ideas.angle: A savings-target piece built on the EBRI finding, aimed at readers within a decade of Medicare enrollment who assume Medicare covers the bill.
story_ideas.hook: A monitored-publisher gap on a headline figure published 03/11/26 that has not been matched.
story_ideas.summary: EBRI Press Release March 11, 2026 2 pages Summary Full Content
story_ideas.consumer: Treat health care as its own line in your retirement plan and check what your projected savings covers against this figure.
story_ideas.b2b: Advisors and insurers selling retirement income products have a number here that reframes the conversation from income replacement to medical liability.
story_ideas.chart: The figures in the finding are the spine of a simple graphic.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.why: A retiree who plans around income alone can be solvent on paper and short on the one expense that does not wait.
story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap; national figure, no state cut available.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Consumer Price Index, medical care, July 2026 — 593.78 index 1982-84=100 (+1.7% year over year)

story_ideas.headline: Whether your state expanded Medicaid still shapes the care you get
story_ideas.angle: A state-by-state read of the KFF expansion tracker for readers approaching 65 without employer coverage, and for the adult children helping them bridge to Medicare.
story_ideas.hook: The interactive tracker refreshed 08/21/26 and remains unmatched by monitored publishers.

story_ideas.headline: The telehealth service you signed up for may have shared what you told it
story_ideas.angle: A consumer-protection piece on the FTC action, joined by Utah and California through Los Angeles County Counsel, alleging a telehealth provider shared sensitive health information with third-party advertising platforms and deceived users about billing and cancellation.
story_ideas.hook: A confirmed gap on a federal enforcement action covering both health-data sharing and subscription cancellation practices.

story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap; national, with two named state participants.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Seven CMS hospice files refreshed between 08/07/26 and 08/19/26, and read together they support something the separate downloads never did — a family can start from a zip code and end at a named, scored provider. Hospice - Zip Data (08/18/26) lists the zip codes each hospice serves. Hospice - General Information (08/19/26) carries address, phone and ownership. Hospice care - Provider CAHPS Hospice Survey Data (08/07/26) gives each provider's scores on the Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems Hospice Survey measures, and the State and National CAHPS files, both refreshed 08/07/26, supply the averages those scores can be judged against. Hospice - Provider Data and Hospice - State Data (08/07/26) add quality of patient care measures at both levels. This is the one cluster in the run that genuinely hangs together, and it has not been worked as a story.

**Why it matters:** A hospice is usually chosen in days, on a name supplied by a discharge planner, and until these files are joined a family has no way to know whether that name is one of several serving their address or the only one, whether its survey scores sit above or below the state mean, or who owns it. The published record now answers all three questions for Medicare-certified hospice providers nationwide, at provider, state and national level. What is at stake is not the file moving; it is that the comparison exists and almost nobody performs it at the moment the decision is made.

**Why pitch this now:** The whole set refreshed inside a thirteen-day window, 08/07/26 to 08/19/26, so provider scores, state means and national means share a vintage and can be joined cleanly. At the next monthly refresh those vintages drift apart again. The nursing home and Medicare-technology threads have carried the last four pitches (09/03/26, 09/04/26, 09/05/26, 09/06/26); the hospice record has sat underneath them untouched.

**Angle:** Whether the hospice a family is handed is the one they would have chosen had they seen the service-area map, the ownership line and the survey scores side by side. Working title: "The Hospice That Serves Your Zip Code." For families arranging end-of-life care on short notice, and for hospice operators whose provider-level scores now sit next to a published state mean.

**Potential headlines:**
- You can look up every hospice that serves your address
- Your state's hospices scored this on the family survey, and one of them is at your bedside
- Who owns the hospice, and why the answer is now published

**Potential outlets:**
- **SeniorLiving.org** — runs state comparisons and lookup-style data studies for readers actively choosing care, which is exactly the form a zip-code-to-provider hospice piece takes.
- **Family Caregiver Alliance** — reaches the caregiver making the hospice call under time pressure, the one reader for whom the service-area file changes a decision.
- **LeadingAge** — nonprofit hospice and LTSS members will want to see how provider CAHPS scores read against the state and national means published alongside them.
- **Fierce Healthcare** — provider and payer readers following Medicare-certified hospice quality reporting and what public scoring at three levels does to referral patterns.
pitch_draft_raw: Seven CMS hospice files refreshed between 08/07/26 and 08/19/26, and read together they support a lookup your readers cannot get anywhere else: enter a zip code, get the hospices whose service area covers it, then check each one's scores on the CAHPS Hospice Survey measures against its state average and the national mean. Hospice - Zip Data carries the service areas, Hospice - General Information carries address, phone and ownership, and the provider, state and national CAHPS files carry the scores, all refreshed within thirteen days of each other so the vintages match. I would write this at about 1,200 words with a state-level table showing where hospice providers sit relative to the national means, plus a short list of what to ask a hospice whose scores fall below its state average. SeniorLiving.org already publishes state comparisons for readers choosing care, and hospice is the choice your audience makes in days rather than months. Everything rests on the published CMS files.
